sections.report:
Walk notes (The whole piece). First read: the eye lands on the bold heading at the top left, then falls into three even grey paragraphs of the same weight. It reads as a plain information page for ferry riders. It feels calm and plain, like a document.

- One-sentence purpose: yes. The heading at (80,75) says it.
- Image and headline make one idea: yes. There's no image.
- Every element does a job: yes. There's no ornament.
- One mood and era: yes.
- Copy finished: yes. No placeholder text or typos.
- Same kind of element looks the same everywhere: yes. The three paragraphs match.
- Mood fits the message: yes. Neutral and calm suits a practical notice.
- Heading names what its section holds: yes.

All lines are yes, so step 5 has no entries to open. One finding sits outside the checklist: the copy is vague exactly where passengers will act on it.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist, from "The words are part of the design": the details passengers will act on can be read more than one way. In paragraph 1 (y≈150) the service runs "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening", which gives no first or last departure. In paragraph 3 (y≈350), "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk" doesn't say which quay (north landing or market quay) or what time. "Every forty minutes" also gives no departure minutes, and the winter months aren't named. A passenger can't plan a trip from this page and has to go to the shelter timetable. If they guess at "late evening" or "before dusk" and guess wrong, they're stranded at the landing. Fix: give the actual first and last departure times from each landing, the winter dates, and the time of the last winter boat from each side. Or point clearly to where the timetable is online, not only to the shelter. Defect. Weight: major, if the page is meant to help people plan crossings.

**What's working.**
- The heading "Notes for ferry passengers" (80,75 to 527,110) is the only bold, large element, and it says exactly what the page is. Anyone knows what they're reading within a second.
- There's no decoration at all: no rules, boxes or colour. The plain, calm look suits a practical service notice, and nothing competes with the text.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The empty band from y≈420 to 800 could be the end of the content or a page that didn't finish loading. Check in a live browser that nothing (a timetable, a map) is missing below the third paragraph.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

First read: my eye lands on the bold headline "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then drops into three body paragraphs of equal weight. It reads as a plain information page for ferry riders. It feels calm and plain. Assumed job: give passengers practical facts about the river ferry (schedule, bicycles, winter changes) that they can read quickly.

Walk, "What matters first":
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. The headline is bold and about twice the body size (y≈72–112).
- Each level of text can be told from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same: **yes**. There are only two levels, a title (about 36 px) and body (about 18 px), and they are far apart.
- Headings differ in weight, form or colour as well as size: **yes**. The title is bold and the body is regular.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The headline at the top left (x≈80–527, y≈72–112) clearly leads. It is roughly twice the body size and bold, so the eye knows where to start and what the page is about before reading a word of the body.
- There are only two text levels, set far apart in both size and weight. Nothing gets in the way of a short notice like this, and the hierarchy never makes the reader wonder which text is a heading.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the type sits in one slab running edge to edge, about x 80–1196 and y 70–415. Everything below y≈415, nearly half the frame, is blank. So the page looks top-heavy and unfinished, as if content failed to load beneath it. The text also gives the eye nowhere to rest beside it, because the only open area is underneath. The cause is the column: it is set the full width of the frame. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance") says a heavy area needs a counterweight. Tschichold's point, that large unexplained empty areas are a fault, applies to the blank lower half. Direction of the fix: narrow the text column to a reading measure of about 600–700 px, still hung from the x≈80 margin. The text then runs further down the frame, and the empty space becomes a deliberate open area on the right. You get a clear asymmetric balance of a dense column against open space, instead of a full slab over a void. This change also fixes the roughly 150-character lines, which the Text critic should be filing separately. Convention (Arnheim on balance). Weight: minor for arrangement alone, since the page can still be read in order. The same change fixes a major line-length problem, so the director may want to merge the two.

**What's working.**
- **Spacing that shows the groups.** The gap under the heading (about 35 px) is clearly larger than the gaps between paragraphs (about 18–20 px), and those are larger than the line spacing. Each paragraph reads as one topic: crossing times, bicycles, winter. The heading clearly sits over all three. Keep these ratios when the column narrows.
- **One left edge.** The heading and all three paragraphs hang exactly from x≈80, with no near-misses and a margin of about 80 px on every side. The page reads as one firm column. Keep that single edge as the anchor when the column narrows.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

I've finished the walk and the reference reads. Writing up the report now.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters? No.** All three paragraphs run from about x=80 to about x=1196 on a 1280 px image. That's roughly 135 to 145 characters per line. The first line, "The river ferry runs … every forty minutes between early morning and late evening. Each", is about 140. Readers have to sweep almost the full screen width on every line and then find the start of the next one. With only about 27 px between lines, it's easy to land on the wrong line on the way back, especially in the first and third paragraphs, which carry the times and the timetable details. The slab also looks heavier and more tiring than three short notes should.
   - **Why:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, §2.1.2, p. 26, gives 45 to 75 characters as the comfortable range for a single column and about 66 as the ideal.
   - **Fix:** Cap the text column at around 65 to 75 characters. At this size that's roughly 600 to 700 px, keeping the left edge at x=80 or centring the column. At that width the current line spacing of about 1.5 is right and can stay. If the full width has to stay, the lines would need noticeably more space between them (Bringhurst §2.2.1; Hochuli, *Detail in Typography*, p. 47). That's the weaker fix.
   - **Type:** Convention, with a real reading cost (defect). **Weight:** major.

**What's working.**
- **Paragraph setting:** The paragraphs are flush left with a soft, even rag. They're separated by space alone, with no indent, and none ends on a lone word. That's clean, standard setting that a reader doesn't notice, which is what it should be. Keep it when narrowing the column.
- **Type scale:** There are just two levels. The bold heading is about twice the size of the body, and the body is a plain sans at about 18 px in near-black on white. It's easy to read, has strong contrast, and leaves no doubt which size does which job.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters).

Walk (Color):
- Small palette: yes. Near-black text on white, nothing else.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. There's no saturated color at all.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark ink on white, with the heading's weight carrying the structure.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. No hues to judge.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. Heading and body text use the same near-black throughout.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. Color carries no meaning here.
- Dark theme uses dark gray: yes. Not a dark theme.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there were no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies, but only barely. This is a single-ink text page (near-black on white) with no hue.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The text is near-black (it looks like a dark charcoal, around #1f2328, not pure #000) on a white ground. That gives strong contrast for long reading without the harshness of pure black on white. The heading and all three paragraphs (x 80–1196, y 75–415) use the same ink, so the color never competes with the reading. Structure comes from weight and size, which suits a plain notice for passengers.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
